subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with high-grade serous ovarian cancer and a germline BRCA2 mutation is started on olaparib after chemotherapy. Her tumor cells cannot repair DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, whereas her nonmalignant cells retain one functional BRCA2 allele.
question: Which of the following best explains why olaparib is selectively toxic to her tumor cells?

options.text: It inhibits topoisomerase II and generates double-strand breaks
It restores BRCA2 function and promotes homologous recombination
It increases DNA methylation of the BRCA2 promoter
It inhibits thymidylate synthase and blocks DNA synthesis
It blocks poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, and the resulting unrepaired single-strand breaks become double-strand breaks that cells lacking homologous recombination cannot repair

explanation_correct: This is synthetic lethality: poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) normally participates in single-strand break repair, and PARP inhibition leaves single-strand breaks that collapse into double-strand breaks at replication forks. Tumor cells lacking BRCA2 cannot repair those breaks by homologous recombination and die, whereas normal cells with intact homologous recombination survive.

explanation_incorrect.A: Topoisomerase II inhibitors such as etoposide and teniposide generate double-strand breaks directly; that is not the mechanism of PARP inhibitors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Olaparib does not restore BRCA function; it exploits the loss of function.
explanation_incorrect.C: DNA methylation changes are not the mechanism of PARP inhibition.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thymidylate synthase is inhibited by 5-fluorouracil, not by PARP inhibitors.

educationalObjective: PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality by producing unrepaired double-strand breaks in BRCA-deficient tumor cells that cannot perform homologous recombination.
